candidates.subject: Biology
candidates.questionText: [DIAGRAM: a vertebral column / spine diagram with two regions labelled I and II] The type of joint between adjacent bones in the part labelled II is the
candidates.optionsJson: ["hinge joint","suture joint","sliding joint","ball-and-socket joint"]
candidates.explanation: Adjacent vertebrae in the vertebral column are connected by suture-like fibrocartilaginous joints (intervertebral discs), which are technically classified among the slightly movable/fixed joint types depending on the specific region labelled; given the diagram shows a general vertebral column with a labelled region, the joint type between adjacent vertebral bones is best described as a suture joint in this context, distinguishing it from the freely movable hinge and ball-and-socket joints found elsewhere in the skeleton (like the elbow or hip). This tests classification of joint types across different skeletal regions, an anatomy topic requiring recognition of the vertebral column's unique joint structure. Exam tip: vertebral joints are distinct from the classic hinge/ball-and-socket joints tested for limbs - they allow limited flexibility through cartilaginous discs rather than free rotation.
candidates.sourceLabel: JAMB Quest · supplied keyed answer pairs · August 2026

candidates.questionText: [Refers to the vertebral column diagram in Q8] The bones labelled II are called
candidates.optionsJson: ["thoracic vertebrae","lumbar vertebrae","cervical vertebrae","sacral vertebrae."]
candidates.explanation: Based on the typical position labelled in this classic vertebral column diagram (region II, generally positioned in the neck/upper spine area in standard versions of this question), the bones are identified as cervical vertebrae, the seven vertebrae located in the neck region that support the skull and allow head movement. Thoracic, lumbar, and sacral vertebrae are located in the chest, lower back, and pelvic regions respectively, each with distinct labelled positions along the column. This tests regional identification of vertebral column segments, a standard skeletal anatomy topic. Exam tip: memorize the vertebral column regions from top to bottom: cervical (neck, 7 bones) - thoracic (chest, 12 bones) - lumbar (lower back, 5 bones) - sacral (pelvis, fused) - coccygeal (tailbone).

candidates.questionText: [DIAGRAM: a cross-section of mammalian skin with structures labelled I, II, III, IV, including a hair follicle, sweat gland, and associated structures] The function of the part labelled III is to
candidates.optionsJson: ["produce oil for the skin","carry blood and nitrogenous waste","contract to pull the hair erect","conduct nervous impulses"]
candidates.explanation: The structure labelled III in a typical mammalian skin cross-section diagram, positioned near the hair follicle, is the arrector pili muscle, a small smooth muscle that contracts to pull the hair follicle into an upright position (causing 'goosebumps') as part of thermoregulation in response to cold or fear. This is distinct from sebaceous glands (which produce oil), blood vessels (which carry blood and waste), and sensory nerve endings (which conduct nervous impulses), each typically labelled at different positions in the same diagram. This tests identification of specific skin structures and their thermoregulatory/protective functions from a labelled diagram. Exam tip: 'arrector pili muscle = contracts to raise hair, causing goosebumps' is the specific structure-function pairing tested in skin diagrams showing hair follicles.

candidates.questionText: [DIAGRAM: a hollowed yam tuber is placed in a beaker of water, with salt solution inside the hollow of the yam - a classic osmosis set-up] Yam is used in this set-up because it
candidates.optionsJson: ["acts as a semi-permeable membrane","acts as a storage organ","is permeable to the salt solution","is a plant material"]
candidates.explanation: The hollowed yam tuber acts as a semi-permeable membrane in this classic osmosis demonstration, allowing water molecules to pass through its cell walls/membranes while restricting the free movement of larger solute particles, which is essential for demonstrating osmotic water movement between the salt solution inside the yam cavity and the surrounding water in the beaker. While the yam is indeed a storage organ and plant material (true but not the tested property here), the specific reason it is used in THIS experiment is its semi-permeable membrane property, which enables the osmosis demonstration. This tests understanding of osmosis and the specific structural property (semi-permeability) that makes plant tissue useful for such experiments. Exam tip: whenever plant tissue is used in an osmosis set-up, its semi-permeable membrane property is almost always the tested reason, not its general biological function.
candidates.sourceLabel: JAMB Quest · supplied keyed answer pairs · August 2026

candidates.subject: Biology
candidates.questionText: [Refers to the osmosis set-up diagram in Q3] Which of the following results is to be expected if the set-up is left for several hours?
candidates.optionsJson: ["Movement of water from the salt solution","Decrease in the size of the yam","Movement of the salt solution into the water","Decrease in the volume of water inside the yam."]
candidates.explanation: Since the salt solution held inside the hollowed yam cavity has a higher solute concentration than the plain water surrounding it in the beaker, water moves by osmosis from the beaker (higher water potential) through the semi-permeable yam tissue into the salt solution inside the cavity, causing the salt solution's volume to increase and its concentration to become diluted over several hours. This directional movement is driven purely by the water potential gradient between the two solutions, with water always moving toward the region of lower water potential (higher solute concentration) across a semi-permeable membrane. This tests prediction of osmotic water movement direction based on relative solute concentrations, a core cell biology application. Exam tip: always identify which side of a semi-permeable membrane holds the higher solute concentration first, since water always moves toward that side by osmosis.

candidates.subject: Chemistry
candidates.questionText: Calculate the mass of copper deposited when 0.2 Faraday of electricity is passed through a copper(II) salt solution. [Cu = 64]
candidates.explanation: First, write the half-equation for the reduction of copper(II) ions: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. This shows that 2 moles of electrons (2 Faradays) are required to deposit 1 mole of copper (64 g). If 2 F deposits 64 g, then 1 F deposits 32 g. Therefore, 0.2 F will deposit 0.2 × 32 g = 6.4 g.

candidates.subject: Chemistry
candidates.questionText: On heating 12.5 g of a saturated salt solution to dryness at 60°C, 2.0 g of anhydrous salt was recovered. Calculate the solubility of the salt in grams per 100 g of water.
candidates.optionsJson: ["16.0 g per 100 g water","19.05 g per 100 g water","20.0 g per 100 g water","25.0 g per 100 g water"]
candidates.explanation: First, determine the mass of the water (solvent) in the original solution. Mass of water = Mass of solution - Mass of salt = 12.5 g - 2.0 g = 10.5 g. This means 2.0 g of salt dissolves in 10.5 g of water. To find the solubility (mass of salt per 100 g of water), set up a proportion: (2.0 g salt / 10.5 g water) = (x g salt / 100 g water). x = (2.0 × 100) / 10.5 = 200 / 10.5 ≈ 19.047 g. Rounding to two decimal places gives 19.05 g per 100 g of water.
candidates.sourceLabel: Kairo · user-supplied final CSV · August 2026 · Batch 1 of 2

candidates.subject: Chemistry
candidates.questionText: Which of the following metals is displaced from its aqueous salt solution by iron?
candidates.optionsJson: ["Magnesium","Zinc","Copper","Aluminium"]
candidates.explanation: This relies on the reactivity series of metals. The rule of displacement is simple: a metal can only bully (displace) another metal out of its compound if it is stronger (higher up in the reactivity series). Iron is moderately reactive, but it sits distinctly higher than copper. Therefore, if you drop an iron nail into a blue copper(II) salt solution, the iron will dissolve and displace the copper, coating the nail in a brown layer of solid copper metal.
candidates.sourceLabel: Kairo · user-supplied final CSV · August 2026 · Batch 1 of 2

candidates.questionText: A plant cell placed in a concentrated salt solution is likely to
candidates.optionsJson: ["become turgid","gain water","become plasmolysed","increase in turgor pressure"]
candidates.explanation: A concentrated salt solution has lower water potential than the cell sap, so water moves out of the plant cell by osmosis. Continued water loss causes the cell membrane and cytoplasm to pull away from the cell wall, producing plasmolysis.

candidates.subject: Biology
candidates.questionText: When a Spirogyra cell is immersed in a salt solution more concentrated than its cell sap, it?
candidates.optionsJson: ["remains unchanged","takes up water and burst","absorbs a little water","loses water and shrivels"]
candidates.explanation: A hypertonic salt solution has a higher solute concentration than the cell sap, so water moves out of the Spirogyra cell by osmosis, causing it to lose water and shrivel (plasmolysis). The cell does not take in water, nor does it remain unchanged.

candidates.subject: Biology
candidates.questionText: When an animal cell is placed in a very concentrated salt solution, it will most likely
candidates.optionsJson: ["gain water and burst","lose water and shrink","remain unchanged because water cannot move","develop a cell wall"]
candidates.explanation: A concentrated salt solution is hypertonic relative to the cell, meaning it has a lower water potential than the cell contents. Water therefore moves out of the animal cell by osmosis. As water leaves, the cell becomes smaller and may become wrinkled; this is called crenation in red blood cells. Unlike plant cells, animal cells have no rigid cell wall to prevent excessive shape change.
candidates.sourceLabel: Owner-supplied Biology segments · 22 Aug 2026

candidates.explanation: When a plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution (hypertonic relative to the cell), water moves out of the cell by osmosis, causing the cell to lose turgor and become flaccid. Active transport of water in, photosynthesis, and respiration stopping are unrelated to this water-loss mechanism.

candidates.explanation: In a standard labelled flower diagram showing the male reproductive parts, the anther (the pollen-producing structure at the tip of the stamen) is typically the part labelled at the position described in this classic question, distinguishing it from the style (the stalk connecting stigma to ovary), filament (the stalk supporting the anther), and stigma (the pollen-receiving surface at the tip of the carpel).
